title: 1 Chronicles 14:1–7
context: 1 Chronicles 14:1–7 parallels 2 Samuel 5:11–16. Hiram of Tyre sends cedar and craftsmen to build David a house, David perceives that the LORD has established his kingdom for Israel’s sake, and Chronicles lists the children born to him in Jerusalem. The two accounts differ in details that are noted rather than harmonized: 2 Samuel 5:13 mentions concubines as well as wives, while 14:3 mentions wives; the Chronicles list has thirteen names, including Elpelet and Nogah, which 2 Samuel 5:14–16 does not list, and Beeliada where Samuel has Eliada. The earlier list in 1 Chronicles 3:5–8 has its own spellings and arrangement. Both traditions read the section as shared ground: the LORD is the one who establishes David’s house, and the king’s exaltation exists for the sake of God’s people.

verses.text: Hiram king of Tyre sent messengers to David with cedar trees, masons, and carpenters, to build him a house.
verses.arminianNotes:
Hiram king of Tyre sends messengers to David with cedar trees, masons, and carpenters to build him a house. The parallel is 2 Samuel 5:11, which Samuel places before the ark story.

Arminian readers see foreign rulers recognizing David’s kingdom, a sign that God was establishing him among the nations, and they note that Chronicles sets this blessing between the two attempts to bring up the ark.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers note that Hiram later supports Solomon as well (1 Kings 5:1), and that the house built for David comes before the question of a house for the LORD in chapter 17.

Both traditions read the verse as part of God’s favor on David’s reign and as shared ground, without pressing the arrangement of material into a doctrine.

verses.text: David perceived that the LORD had established him king over Israel, for his kingdom was highly exalted, for his people Israel’s sake.
verses.arminianNotes:
David perceives that the LORD has established him king over Israel, for his kingdom is highly exalted, for the sake of God’s people Israel. The parallel in 2 Samuel 5:12 is very close.

Arminian readers see David rightly understanding that his kingship is a trust held for the good of the people, not a possession for his own glory, and they see this humility as part of faithful leadership.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers stress the phrase “for his people Israel’s sake” and note that the king exists for the sake of God’s people and that God, not David, is the source of his exalted position.

Both traditions read the verse as a model of humble leadership that acknowledges God as the giver of authority, and both treat it as shared ground.

verses.text: David took more wives in Jerusalem, and David became the father of more sons and daughters.
verses.arminianNotes:
David takes more wives in Jerusalem and becomes the father of more sons and daughters. The parallel in 2 Samuel 5:13 also mentions concubines.

Arminian readers note the narrator’s restraint, and many connect the verse with the law’s warning that a king “shall not multiply wives to himself” (Deuteronomy 17:17), a warning whose cost appears later in the troubles of David’s family.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers note that Chronicles records the fact without comment and does not mention concubines here, though 3:9 refers to sons of concubines, and they read the verse as an honest record rather than approval.

Both traditions treat the verse as a sober record of a godly king’s household and avoid building doctrine on the differences between the accounts.

verses.text: These are the names of the children whom he had in Jerusalem: Shammua, Shobab, Nathan, Solomon,
verses.arminianNotes:
The children born to David in Jerusalem include Shammua, Shobab, Nathan, and Solomon. The earlier list in 3:5 spells the first name Shimea and names the mother Bathshua.

Arminian readers note that Solomon, who will succeed David, appears here among his brothers without special notice, and they read the list as an honest record of a growing royal family.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers note that both Solomon and Nathan appear later in the genealogies of Jesus (Matthew 1:6; Luke 3:31), and they see God’s purposes for David’s line at work in ways not yet visible in this list.

Both traditions read the names as historical record and as part of Chronicles’ attention to David’s house, and they treat it as shared ground.

verses.arminianNotes:
The list continues with Ibhar, Elishua, and Elpelet. Elpelet does not appear in the parallel list in 2 Samuel 5:15, and the list in 3:6 has different names at this point.

Arminian readers see the genealogical detail as part of a real historical record, and they note that the differences between the lists can be acknowledged honestly without being forced into agreement.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers agree that the lists differ in length and spelling, and they hold that the authority of Scripture does not depend on resolving every variation in name lists, so the differences are noted rather than harmonized.

Both traditions treat the verse as historical record and do not build doctrine on the variations among the lists in Samuel and Chronicles.

verses.arminianNotes:
The list continues with Nogah, Nepheg, and Japhia. Nogah is absent from the parallel list in 2 Samuel 5:15 but appears in the earlier Chronicles list at 3:7.

Arminian readers note that Chronicles preserves names that Samuel does not record, and they see in this the Chronicler’s care to give a fuller account of David’s household for his own readers.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers note that even the sons who play no further role in the story are named, which reflects the importance of David’s house in God’s purposes, a theme that becomes central in the promise of chapter 17.

Both traditions read the names simply as record and leave the differences between the lists as they stand, without forcing them together.

verses.arminianNotes:
The list ends with Elishama, Beeliada, and Eliphelet. The parallel in 2 Samuel 5:16 and the list in 3:8 both read Eliada where this verse has Beeliada.

Arminian readers note that some interpreters suggest the two names are forms of one name, but the text does not say so, and they prefer to record the difference rather than to settle it by conjecture.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers see the end of the list as preparing for the promise concerning David’s offspring in chapter 17, where God himself undertakes to build David a house.

Both traditions treat the variation between Beeliada and Eliada as a matter for careful study rather than doctrine, and they read the list as shared ground about the growth of David’s household.
